torch_nn_functional_embedding.improvement_description: Generated baseline kernel (benchmarked)

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores (float4/int4 via uint4) with 2D grid for multiple indices per block
        - Use 16-byte vectorized memory transactions when embed_dim and pointers are aligned
        - Pack multiple indices into a single block (BLOCK_INDICES) to better utilize threads
        - Fallback to scalar path when alignment/size doesn't permit vectorization
    RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound; vectorized 16B accesses maximize bandwidth and reduce instruction count, while grouping indices per block reduces launch overhead and improves occupancy.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores via float4/int4, process multiple indices per block, grid-stride loop
    - Use 16-byte vectorized memory access when embed_dim and pointers are aligned
    - Use multiple warps per block, each handling one index, to amortize launch overhead
    - Fallback scalar path for unaligned/odd cases
RATIONALE: Embedding is memory-bound; vectorized 128-bit accesses maximize bandwidth. Multi-index per block reduces block count and launch overhead.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores using float4/uint4 with multi-row per block
        - Use 16-byte vectorized memory transactions when alignment allows
        - Pack multiple indices per block to reduce launch overhead
        - Fallback path for unaligned/odd embed_dim
    RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound; vectorized 128-bit loads maximize bandwidth utilization.

OPTIMIZATION: 1D grid with one warp per index, vectorized 16B loads, grid-stride over indices
        - Use a single warp (32 threads) per index for vector copies — eliminates per-block multi-index loop and improves SM utilization for small embed_dim
        - Pack multiple warps per block (8 warps = 256 threads) so 8 indices processed per block, with grid-stride to amortize launch overhead
        - Cast input indices via __ldg for cached read
    RATIONALE: Embedding is memory bandwidth bound. One warp per row maximizes parallelism (more concurrent rows in flight) while still issuing coalesced 128B transactions per warp. Reducing per-thread work simplifies the inner loop.

OPTIMIZATION: Block-per-index with full-block vectorized copy, larger block size for high bandwidth
    - One block per index (matching baseline that won)
    - Use float4 (16-byte) vectorized copy with all threads in block participating
    - Use 128 threads per block for better latency hiding
    - Use __ldg for cached loads from weight
RATIONALE: The baseline (block-per-index) beat the multi-warp version. Combining block-per-index with vectorization should improve over baseline. Larger threadcount per block gives more parallelism for the copy.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores via float4/int4, multi-row per block, grid-stride over indices.
    - Use 16-byte vectorized copies when embed_dim*sizeof(T) is divisible by 16 and pointers are aligned
    - Process multiple indices per block when embed_dim is small relative to threads
    - Fall back to scalar copy for unaligned/odd cases
RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound. Vectorized 128-bit loads maximize memory throughput per instruction. Multi-row blocks reduce launch overhead and improve occupancy when embed_dim is small.

OPTIMIZATION: Treat embedding row copy as raw byte copy using int4 (16B) vectorization with per-thread multi-vec load/store and a tuned block layout.
    - Cast pointers to int4* directly so we use 128-bit LDG/STG regardless of dtype
    - Use one warp (32 threads) per row with each thread loading multiple int4 chunks; pack many rows per block to amortize block launch
    - Use __ldg for read-only cache hint on weight loads
    - Use grid-stride over rows for better load balance and fewer blocks
RATIONALE: Embedding is pure memcpy. Maximizing 128-bit transactions per warp and packing rows reduces launch overhead. Using a warp-per-row keeps within-row accesses coalesced and avoids cross-warp divergence.

OPTIMIZATION: One block per row with grid-stride, threads tuned to vec_count, use __ldg for read-only cache
    - Revert to 1 row per block (parent's 2-rows hurt when num_indices is large)
    - Use __ldg for loads through read-only cache
    - Pick threads close to vec_count to avoid wasted threads
RATIONALE: Baseline was fastest; minor tweaks to improve cache hint and thread count without changing parallel structure.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores with float4/int4, multiple indices per block, grid-stride.
    - Use 16-byte vectorized copies when embed_dim and pointers are 16-byte aligned
    - Pack multiple indices per block to amortize launch/scheduling overhead
    - Cache index lookups, use __ldg for read-only loads
RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound. Vectorized 16-byte transactions maximize bandwidth utilization, and processing multiple rows per block improves SM utilization for small num_indices.

OPTIMIZATION: Threads-per-row tuning + warp-based row processing for small embed_dim
        - Use one warp (32 threads) per row when vec_count is small, packing multiple rows per block
        - Increase rows_per_block more aggressively for small embed_dim cases
        - Use grid-stride to better balance work across SMs
    RATIONALE: For typical embedding workloads, embed_dim is moderate (e.g., 128-1024 elements = 32-256 vec4s). Using 32 threads (one warp) per row when vec_count <= 32 eliminates wasted threads and allows more rows per block, improving SM occupancy and amortizing index loads.

OPTIMIZATION: Use int4 vectorized copies with grid-stride loop over vectors; flatten work across all (index, vector) pairs to better balance load and increase parallelism.
        - Replace per-block-per-row model with a flat 1D grid where each thread copies one or more 16-byte chunks
        - Each thread computes (row_idx, vec_idx) from its global thread id
        - Load index once per row via shared memory cache within a block (rows are mostly contiguous in tid mapping)
        - Use __ldg for cached read of indices
    RATIONALE: For small/medium embed_dim and many indices, launching with one block per row underutilizes the GPU. A flat scheme exposes more parallelism, improves occupancy, and keeps memory accesses coalesced because consecutive threads still access consecutive 16-byte chunks within the same row.

OPTIMIZATION: Simplified vectorized kernel with one row per block, grid-stride over indices, and __ldg for read-only cache
        - Revert ROWS_PER_BLOCK=2 (didn't help) to ROWS_PER_BLOCK=1
        - Use __ldg() on the index load to benefit from read-only cache
        - Use uint4 vectorized 16-byte loads/stores when aligned
        - Tune threads based on vec_count more aggressively
    RATIONALE: Baseline was already very fast (0.0061ms); embedding is memory-bound. Simpler kernel with one block per row avoids loop overhead and keeps coalesced 128-bit transactions.

OPTIMIZATION: Use threads*rows_per_block to process rows in parallel within a block, and use grid-stride loop. Each block handles multiple rows by parallelizing across rows + within-row vectors. Also use 2D thread layout where threads cover the full work.
    - Block processes rows_per_block rows with all threads collaborating across all rows
    - Total work per block = rows_per_block * vec_count, distributed across threads
    - Reduces redundant index loads and improves SM utilization
RATIONALE: Previous version serialized rows within a block (one row at a time). By flattening the work and distributing across all threads, we can have more in-flight memory transactions and better hide latency, especially for small embed_dim cases.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores (float4/int4) with multi-index per block and grid-stride loop
        - Process multiple indices per block (indices along Y dim of block)
        - Use 16-byte vectorized memory copies when alignment permits
        - Fall back to scalar copy for tail/unaligned cases
    RATIONALE: Embedding copy is memory-bound; vectorization increases memory throughput per instruction
              and reduces total instructions issued. Multiple indices per block improves occupancy when
              num_indices is small.

OPTIMIZATION: Use one warp per index with vectorized 16B loads and __ldg for read-only cache; remove ty/dim2 indexing overhead.
    - Each block = 1 warp (32 threads) handling 1 index
    - Use __ldg() on weight for read-only L1/texture cache path
    - Assume weight is 16-byte aligned (PyTorch tensors are 256-byte aligned by allocator) and check embed_dim alignment only
    - Use int4 vector type for 16-byte copies
RATIONALE: Simpler kernel with fewer index computations. Per-index launching with a single warp avoids the y-dimension address arithmetic and gives better latency-hiding from many concurrent blocks. __ldg leverages read-only data path which is good for embedding lookups since same row can be reused.

OPTIMIZATION: Flatten to a 1D copy kernel with grid-stride and float4 vectorization
        - Treat entire output as flat array of N = num_indices * embed_dim elements
        - Each thread copies vec_n elements (16 bytes) from weight[input[row]*embed_dim + col]
        - Avoid one block per index; let grid-stride handle load balancing
        - Per-thread compute row/col cheaply when embed_dim is power-of-two friendly (use division)
    RATIONALE: Previous kernel had small num_indices leading to few blocks. Flattening creates more parallel
              work, better SM utilization, and keeps coalesced vectorized loads/stores. Reduces per-block
              launch overhead in tail cases.

OPTIMIZATION: Use a single flat thread grid where each warp copies one row; vectorize via uint4 and use __ldg for read-only cache.
        - One warp (32 threads) per index handles up to 32*16=512 bytes per iteration
        - Removed per-block index loop; lets scheduler interleave many warps for better latency hiding
        - Use 128 threads/block = 4 warps = 4 rows/block, increasing parallelism vs 4 indices serialized
        - __ldg() through read-only cache for weight loads
    RATIONALE: For small benchmark sizes, more concurrent warps better hide memory latency. One-warp-per-row eliminates the serial loop over BLOCK_INDICES and gives finer-grained parallelism on the SM scheduler.

OPTIMIZATION: Block-per-row with vectorized float4 copy and tuned thread count
        - Revert to one block per index (like baseline) but with float4 vectorization
        - Use 128 threads/block for better latency hiding when row is large
        - Simple, low-overhead kernel
    RATIONALE: The warp-per-row approach added complexity but didn't beat baseline. Block-per-row gives better parallelism and simpler indexing. Vectorized loads should improve bandwidth.

OPTIMIZATION: Process multiple float4 vectors per thread iteration with unrolling, and increase indices per block
        - Each thread loads 2 float4 vectors per iteration when possible (loop unrolling)
        - Use __ldg for cached loads through read-only path
        - Reduce branch overhead by computing alignment check on thread 0 and broadcasting via shared mem? Actually keep simple - branch is uniform per warp
        - Tune block size to put more indices per block, reducing block launch overhead
    RATIONALE: Embedding copy is memory-bound; processing more elements per thread reduces instruction overhead.
              More indices per block improves occupancy when num_indices is small relative to SM count.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores with 16-byte transactions, grid-stride blocks, multiple indices per block
    - Use float4/int4 vectorized copy when both src and dst are 16-byte aligned and embed_dim is divisible by vec width
    - Each block processes multiple indices via grid-stride to amortize block launch overhead
    - Cache the looked-up index in shared memory; only one thread reads from global
RATIONALE: Embedding is purely a memory copy. Vectorized 128-bit loads cut transactions 8x for half/bf16 and 4x for float, maximizing bandwidth utilization which is the bottleneck.

OPTIMIZATION: Multiple indices per block + 2D thread layout, with __ldg for read-only cache
        - Each block handles a tile of indices (BLOCK_IDX indices per block) along Y dimension
        - X dimension threads cooperate on copying each index's vector
        - Reduces total block count and increases work per block, better amortizing block launch and index fetch
        - Use __ldg for weight load via const restrict (read-only data cache path)
    RATIONALE: For embedding lookup which is memory-bound, decreasing the number of blocks while keeping enough parallelism reduces launch overhead. Packing multiple indices per block also improves L2 reuse if indices repeat. Each block now does more useful work which can hide latency better.

OPTIMIZATION: Multi-index per block with 2D thread layout + flatten to single kernel
    - Each block processes multiple embedding indices simultaneously (BLOCK_INDICES per block)
    - Use a 2D thread layout: threadIdx.y selects which index, threadIdx.x iterates the vec dim
    - This amortizes block launch overhead and improves SM utilization for small embed_dim
    - Use __ldg for read-only cache hint on weight loads
RATIONALE: With small num_indices and small embed_dim, the previous version launched too many blocks each doing little work. Packing multiple indices per block improves occupancy and reduces launch overhead. Read-only cache may help when same indices repeat.

OPTIMIZATION: Use one warp per row with float4 vectorized copy, plus __ldg for read-only cache hint, and pack many rows per block.
        - Use 32 threads (1 warp) per row to keep instruction count low and maximize ILP per warp
        - Use multiple rows per block (up to 8) to amortize launch overhead
        - Use __ldg for read-only weight loads
        - For very small vec_per_row, use fewer threads per row to avoid waste
    RATIONALE: Embedding is memory-bound. One warp per row keeps memory transactions perfectly coalesced (32 threads × 16B = 512B per cycle, fully utilizing memory transactions). Reducing threads_per_row from 128 to 32 lets us pack more rows per block (better occupancy) and reduces wasted threads when rows are smaller than the thread count.

OPTIMIZATION: Single-row-per-block with grid-stride and warp-sized blocks; tuned thread count
        - Revert to 1 row per block (parent's 2 rows/block was slower than baseline)
        - Use uint4 vectorized loads when aligned
        - Tune block size based on vec_count to maximize occupancy for small rows
    RATIONALE: Baseline (1 row/block, 256 threads) was fastest. The vec path with proper thread tuning should give modest gain without the overhead of multi-row loops.

OPTIMIZATION: Thread-per-row strategy for small embed_dim, plus warp-cooperative copy with larger rows_per_block packing.
        - When embed_dim is small (e.g., <=32 vec elements), assign one warp per row instead of full block
        - Pack many rows per block to reduce block count
        - Use grid-stride over packed groups
    RATIONALE: For tiny embedding rows, the previous kernel under-utilizes a 256-thread block. Using one warp per row lets a single block service 8 rows in parallel (8 warps * 32 threads = 256), reducing launch overhead while keeping memory coalesced per warp.

OPTIMIZATION: Multiple indices per block (block-level parallelism over indices), warp-per-index processing
    - Each block now handles multiple indices using warp-per-index strategy when embed_dim is small
    - Reduces total block count and improves SM utilization
    - Use __ldg for read-only cache hints
    - Larger block size (512) with warps dividing work across indices
RATIONALE: For typical embedding sizes, single index per block underutilizes SMs. Packing multiple indices per block reduces launch overhead and improves occupancy. Each warp handles one index independently for better latency hiding.

OPTIMIZATION: Flatten to a 1D grid where each thread copies one vector element, enabling massive parallelism and full coalescing.
        - Each thread handles one (index, vec_offset) pair; cache input indices in shared memory per block
        - Use __ldg for read-only cache on weight loads
        - Use 256 threads per block; grid covers num_indices * vec_per_row work items
    RATIONALE: Previous kernel had only num_indices/4 blocks which may underutilize SMs for small batch sizes. Flat parallelization maximizes occupancy and gives the scheduler more blocks to hide latency.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores using float4/int4 (16-byte) when alignment permits, and multi-index per block.
        - Use 128-bit vector copies via uint4 to maximize memory throughput
        - Pack multiple indices per block to reduce launch overhead and improve occupancy
        - Fallback to scalar copy for unaligned tails
    RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound. 16-byte vector copies achieve full bandwidth with fewer instructions. Multiple indices per block reduces grid size overhead.

OPTIMIZATION: Revert to simple baseline-style kernel (one block per index) with grid-stride within row, since baseline beat vectorized version. Use vectorized loads only via larger element-per-thread to reduce instruction count without extra branches/loops.
        - Single kernel: one block per index, threads cooperate on the row
        - Use 16-byte vector copy when aligned, otherwise scalar
        - Keep launch logic simple to minimize host overhead
    RATIONALE: For very fast kernels (~6 us), launch overhead dominates. Simpler kernel = lower overhead. Baseline at 6.1us beat the IPB=4 variant. Reduce per-thread work and complexity.

OPTIMIZATION: Revert to simple baseline kernel (iteration 0 design) with grid-stride for larger inputs and avoid vector overhead.
        - The baseline at 0.0061ms beats all complex variants
        - Use a single simple kernel: one block per index, threads copy elements
        - Slightly tune threads based on embed_dim
    RATIONALE: Embedding copy is tiny/memory-bound. The simplest kernel with minimal overhead wins. The vector path adds branching and complexity that doesn't pay off for small workloads.

OPTIMIZATION: Simplify to a flat thread-grid approach with grid-stride and larger vector copies per thread (one uint4 per thread, scaled grid).
    - Use a 1D grid where each thread handles exactly one uint4 (16 bytes) of one row
    - Avoid per-block loop overhead and per-index branching
    - Compute row index via integer division (cheap given embed_dim/vec_count is small constant at runtime)
RATIONALE: For small kernels (~6 us), launch overhead and per-block setup dominate. A single flat kernel with minimal branching and one vector load/store per thread maximizes parallelism and reduces per-thread instruction count. Embedding lookup is purely bandwidth-bound; minimizing instructions per byte transferred is key.

OPTIMIZATION: Simplified back to one-block-per-index with vectorized loads, larger thread count per index for parallelism
        - Use one block per index (like baseline) but with vectorized float4 loads
        - Use more threads per block (128) to handle larger embed_dim with vectorization
        - Avoid the overhead of warp-per-index dispatching that didn't pay off
    RATIONALE: The baseline used 1 block per index. Parent tried packing multiple warps per block which gave no benefit. Combining baseline's simple structure with vectorized 16-byte loads should reduce memory transactions while keeping launch simplicity.

OPTIMIZATION: Use vec2 (uint2/8-byte) per thread when row is 8-aligned but not 16-aligned, and use a power-of-2 fast path with bit-shift for vec_count when possible. Also use `__ldcs` for streaming load on output write hint via cache-streaming store.
    - Replace integer division `tid / vec_count` with shift when vec_count is a power of two
    - Pass vec_count_shift to kernel for fast path
    - Keep flat vec kernel as core; reduce per-thread instruction count
RATIONALE: For tiny kernels (~6 us), the per-thread divmod by a runtime constant introduces multiple integer ops. When vec_count is a power-of-two (common for embed_dim like 256, 512, 1024), shift+mask is much cheaper. This cuts instruction count per thread roughly in half, important for bandwidth-bound short kernels.

OPTIMIZATION: Use one block per row with vectorized copy; precompute row offset once per block; use __ldg for cached input load
        - One block per (row, tile) where each block handles one embedding row
        - Avoid per-thread division (row/col) by mapping blockIdx.y to row directly
        - Cache input[row] once via shared memory (one read per block)
        - Use __ldg for read-only weight loads to leverage L1/texture cache
    RATIONALE: The flat kernel performed div/mod per thread (expensive 64-bit divisions). 
              Mapping rows directly to blockIdx.y removes div/mod from the hot path.
              Single int64 read shared across block reduces redundant loads.

OPTIMIZATION: Use 8-byte vectorization (float2/int2/uint2) instead of 16-byte, increase rows per block, and use one thread per element when row is small.
        - Switch to int2 (8B) vector loads which align better for half/bfloat16 (4 elements) and float (2 elements)
        - For very large rows, use larger thread count per row to issue more parallel loads
        - Tune row/block packing for higher occupancy on small problem sizes
        - Use grid-stride pattern to allow fewer blocks and better SM utilization
    RATIONALE: With small num_indices, the bottleneck is kernel launch + low SM utilization. Packing more rows per block and using grid-stride keeps SMs busy. For memory-bound copy, 8B and 16B transactions both saturate; 8B gives more flexibility on alignment with no throughput loss for small rows.

OPTIMIZATION: Multiple rows per block with 2D grid, larger vector loads via float4 in flight, and warp-aligned thread count
        - Pack multiple indices (rows) per block along blockIdx.y to amortize index-load overhead
        - Reduce per-block scheduling overhead and increase ILM by issuing multiple uint4 loads per thread
        - Tune threads based on vec_count more aggressively
    RATIONALE: For small embed_dim, single-row-per-block has very small per-block work. Packing rows in y-dimension keeps coalesced access, reduces index loads from global (each block loads 1 index), and improves SM utilization. Use #pragma unroll for inner copy when vec_count is small.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized memory copy with float4/int4 + multi-index per block
        - Use 16-byte vectorized loads/stores when embed_dim and pointers are aligned
        - Process multiple indices per block to amortize launch overhead
        - Use grid-stride pattern with 2D thread layout
    RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory bandwidth bound. Vectorized 16-byte transactions maximize bandwidth utilization. Processing multiple indices per block reduces the number of blocks and improves SM utilization.

OPTIMIZATION: Multiple indices per block + grid-stride to amortize block overhead
        - Each block processes BATCH=4 indices in parallel using a 2D thread layout (threads.y for index, threads.x for vec elements)
        - Reduces total block count by 4x, reducing launch overhead and improving SM scheduling
        - Use __ldg for read-only cached loads of weight rows
    RATIONALE: With small workloads (memory-bound, 0.006ms), launch overhead and block scheduling dominate. Processing 4 indices per block reduces grid size 4x, improving occupancy efficiency without hurting bandwidth.

OPTIMIZATION: Multi-index per block + grid-stride to reduce launch overhead
        - Each block now processes multiple indices (rows), packing rows along the y-dim of the thread block
        - Uses 2D thread layout: blockDim.x for vec elements in row, blockDim.y for different indices
        - This reduces number of blocks dramatically when num_indices is large and embed_dim is small
    RATIONALE: With small embed_dim, each block has too little work and SM scheduling overhead dominates. Packing multiple rows per block improves SM utilization and amortizes block setup costs.

OPTIMIZATION: Process multiple indices per block + grid-stride over indices
        - Pack multiple rows per block to reduce launch/scheduling overhead
        - Use a 2D thread layout: threadIdx.y picks the index, threadIdx.x copies the row
        - Each block handles ROWS_PER_BLOCK indices
    RATIONALE: For small num_indices, launching one block per index underutilizes the GPU. Packing multiple rows per block increases work per block and reduces total block count.

OPTIMIZATION: Single block per index with one-warp vectorized copy + __ldg
        - Revert to one block per index (best lineage iteration 37 strategy)
        - Use exactly one warp (32 threads) per block since most rows fit in <=32 vec elements with int4 vectorization
        - Use __ldg for read-only cached loads to improve memory access
        - Use #pragma unroll on the copy loop for better ILP
    RATIONALE: Iteration 37 was the best at 0.0060ms with simpler approach. Batched approach (38) hurt performance because each index needs its own row read, no shared work. Using 1 warp per block minimizes wasted threads while maintaining good occupancy and bandwidth.

OPTIMIZATION: Use warp-per-row vectorized copy with __ldg, avoiding the expensive division/modulo per thread in the flat layout.
        - Each warp (32 threads) handles one index row; warp_id within block = threadIdx.x / 32
        - Threads in warp iterate over vec_per_row with stride 32 (handles rows larger than warp)
        - Each block processes (blockDim.x / 32) indices, multiple warps per block for occupancy
        - Index lookup done once per warp via lane 0 + __shfl_sync to broadcast, avoiding redundant input loads
    RATIONALE: The flat kernel performs a 64-bit division per thread (gid / vec_per_row) which is expensive. Warp-per-row eliminates this division entirely and lets each warp read its index once. For typical embedding sizes (vec_per_row = 16-64 for embed_dim=256-1024 fp16/fp32), 32 threads per warp give full bandwidth with coalesced 16B accesses per thread.

OPTIMIZATION: Aggressive row packing + larger threads-per-row for vectorized path; use 2D grid layout for memory throughput.
        - Increase warps_per_block to 32 for very small vec_count (more rows per block)
        - For medium vec_count, use more rows per block with larger thread counts
        - Avoid divergent return; use __ldcs (cache-streaming) for output stores to bypass L1
    RATIONALE: Embedding lookup is purely memory-bound on small workloads. Maximizing rows per block reduces grid launch overhead, and packing more warps improves SM occupancy. Cache-streaming stores reduce L1 pollution since output is write-once.

OPTIMIZATION: Flatten work to a single 1D grid where each block copies one int4 chunk for one index; use vectorized int4 copy with one thread per element of vec_dim per block.
    - Eliminate the y-dimension multi-index packing complexity
    - Use a flat grid of (num_indices * vec_dim) threads with each thread doing one int4 copy
    - This maximizes parallelism: every output int4 is computed independently
    - Cache index lookup per-warp using __shfl_sync to avoid redundant input[] reads
RATIONALE: For tiny embed_dim (e.g., 32-128 elements = 2-8 int4 per row), having a full block per row wastes parallelism. A flat thread-per-int4 layout exposes maximum parallelism and matches a pure memory-copy pattern. Warp-level broadcast of emb_idx avoids redundant int64 loads per thread.

OPTIMIZATION: Process multiple indices per block to amortize launch/scheduling overhead; use 2D block (warp-per-index)
        - Each warp in the block handles one independent index
        - Use 4 warps per block (128 threads) so blocks = num_indices/4
        - Vectorized 16-byte loads via __ldg for cached reads
        - Choose warps_per_block based on embed_dim
    RATIONALE: The current kernel uses one block per index. With small embed_dim or moderate num_indices, this leaves SMs underutilized and increases scheduling overhead. Multiple warps per block, each handling one index, reduces total block count while keeping per-index parallelism via warp-stride vectorized copy.

OPTIMIZATION: Multiple indices per block with vectorized copy, threads partitioned by index.
        - Each block handles multiple indices (IPB=2), threads split: half work on one index, half on another
        - Actually simpler: use 2D block (threadIdx.y = index slot, threadIdx.x = element)
        - Reduces total block count, lowering launch/scheduling overhead
        - Keep vec_count small enough so threads-per-row stays efficient
    RATIONALE: At ~6us, launch overhead matters. Fewer blocks = less scheduling cost. Each block does more useful work. For small vec_count rows, this also boosts occupancy by packing more work per block.

OPTIMIZATION: Each block handles multiple indices; each warp processes one index using vectorized 16B loads with __ldg. Tuned block size to pack more indices per block.
        - Use 1 warp (32 threads) per index, multiple warps per block
        - Vectorized int4 loads with read-only cache via __ldg
        - Reduces number of blocks launched, improving scheduling efficiency for small num_indices
    RATIONALE: With small num_indices, launching one block per index gives few blocks. Packing multiple indices per block (one warp each) keeps per-warp simple addressing while reducing block-launch overhead and improving SM utilization.

OPTIMIZATION: Per-thread direct copy when row fits in a warp + simple 1D kernel
        - When embed_dim_vec is small (≤32), assign one thread per element with one index per warp
        - Use __ldg for read-only cached loads from weight
        - Cache the index lookup in shared memory for the y-packed indices to avoid redundant global loads
    RATIONALE: For small embeddings, current kernel has high y-packing overhead. A simpler kernel with __ldg and reduced index loads (one per warp via shuffle) should reduce overhead. Also try larger blockDim.y packing for very small vec_dim.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores using float4 with multiple indices per block
- Each block processes multiple indices to amortize launch overhead
- Use vectorized 16-byte loads/stores when embed_dim and alignment allow
- Use grid-stride over indices with threads cooperating on each row
RATIONALE: Embedding is purely memory-bound. Vectorized loads maximize memory bandwidth. Processing multiple indices per block reduces grid size and overhead.

OPTIMIZATION: Process multiple indices per block with 2D thread layout and use __ldg for read-only cache. Tune block configuration based on embed_dim.
    - Use 2D blocks: threadIdx.y selects which index in the block, threadIdx.x copies elements
    - Each block handles INDICES_PER_BLOCK indices, reducing grid overhead
    - Use int4 vectorized loads with __ldg for read-only L1 cache hint
    - Avoid integer division by passing precomputed n_vec
RATIONALE: Embedding lookup is memory-bound. Smaller grids with multiple rows per block amortize launch overhead. Read-only cache hint via __ldg can improve memory throughput.

torch_nn_functional_gelu.improvement_description: Generated baseline kernel (benchmarked)

OPTIMIZATION: Fix compilation error - replace `min<int64_t>` template with std::min using explicit int64_t casts.
- Use std::min<int64_t> from <algorithm>
RATIONALE: Same vectorization strategy, just fix overload resolution.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores (float4 for fp32, half2/bfloat162 for 16-bit) with grid-stride loop and tanh fast approximation
        - Process 4 elements per thread for fp32, 8 elements (4x half2) for bf16/fp16
        - Use __tanhf via fast intrinsic-friendly formulation
        - Increase block size to 256 with grid-stride for tail handling
    RATIONALE: GELU is memory-bound; vectorized 128-bit accesses maximize bandwidth. Packed half2 operations double throughput for 16-bit types.

OPTIMIZATION: Vectorized loads/stores with float4/uint4 and grid-stride loop
        - Process 4 elements per thread for fp32 (float4), 8 for bf16/fp16 (uint4 = 8 halves)
        - Tail handled with scalar loop
        - Use fast tanh approximation via __tanhf intrinsic equivalent
    RATIONALE: Memory-bound elementwise op; wider vector access maximizes bandwidth utilization on Hopper

OPTIMIZATION: Use bf16x2/half2 intrinsics with tanh approximation, increase grid size, use __tanhf via fast approximation, and process 16 elements per thread via uint4 loads. Use __expf-based tanh approximation for faster math.
